nameStory: This tiny marine creature doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Hyperia galba. The name 'Hyperia' comes from Greek mythology, referencing Hyperion, one of the Titans associated with light and observation - fitting for a creature with notably large eyes that help it navigate the ocean's depths.
description: Hyperia galba is a microscopic marine animal that belongs to a group called amphipods - tiny shrimp-like creatures that are part of the ocean's zooplankton community. These translucent animals are smaller than your pinky nail and spend their lives drifting through New England's coastal waters. They have a distinctive curved body shape and proportionally enormous eyes that take up much of their head, giving them an almost alien appearance when viewed under magnification.

idTips.label: Enormous eyes
idTips.description: The eyes are disproportionately huge compared to the body size, appearing as dark, bulging domes that can take up nearly half the head area when viewed under a hand lens

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The entire body appears glassy and see-through, with internal organs sometimes visible as shadowy shapes beneath the clear exterior

idTips.label: Curved posture
idTips.description: The body naturally curls into a C-shape when disturbed, like a tiny glass comma floating in the water

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with jerky, darting motions using rapid beats of small leg-like appendages, quite different from the smooth gliding of other zooplankton

habitat: Found in New England's coastal and offshore waters, particularly in areas where ocean currents bring nutrient-rich water close to shore. They're most commonly encountered in deeper waters beyond the continental shelf but can occasionally be found in samples from harbors and bays during certain weather conditions.

seasonality.spring: Numbers begin to increase in coastal waters as ocean temperatures rise and plankton blooms provide abundant food sources.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when they're most likely to be found in plankton samples from New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Still present but numbers decline as water temperatures drop and they move to deeper, more stable water layers.
seasonality.winter: Rare in surface waters, having moved to deeper ocean layers where temperatures remain more constant throughout the cold months.

funFact: Despite being smaller than a grain of rice, Hyperia galba has some of the proportionally largest eyes in the animal kingdom - they're so big that if humans had eyes of the same relative size, each eye would be the size of a dinner plate!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiny transparent zooplankton, but the enormous eyes make Hyperia galba unmistakable once you know what to look for - no other common New England zooplankton has eyes that dominate the head to such an extreme degree.
contextualKnowledge: This creature represents the hidden microscopic world that supports all marine life in New England waters. Though invisible to the naked eye individually, these tiny animals form the crucial link between microscopic algae and larger fish, making them essential to the ocean food web despite their tiny size.
compareHints: While there are no other Hyperia species commonly found in New England waters, this species can be distinguished from other amphipods in the region by its pelagic (open ocean) lifestyle rather than bottom-dwelling habits. Unlike coastal amphipods that scuttle along the seafloor, Hyperia galba is adapted for life in the open water column with its streamlined body and powerful swimming appendages.
